back: A functional unit of nature in which living organisms interact among themselves and with the surrounding physical environment.
The vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels in an ecosystem (e.g., trees → shrubs → herbs).
The rate of production of organic matter by autotrophs during photosynthesis.
GPP minus respiration losses (GPP – R); the biomass available to heterotrophs.
The rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers (assimilation of ingested food energy).
Dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) plus dead animal remains and faecal matter; the raw material for decomposition.
Breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores such as earthworms.
Movement of water-soluble inorganic nutrients down the soil horizon, where they may precipitate as unavailable salts.
Degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes.
Formation of a dark, colloidal, microbe-resistant humus that acts as a nutrient reservoir; decomposes very slowly.
Further microbial degradation of humus, releasing inorganic nutrients back for reuse by producers.
Green plants (and photosynthetic bacteria) that fix solar energy to make food; first trophic level.
Herbivores that feed directly on producers (second trophic level).
Carnivores that eat primary consumers (third trophic level).
A food chain beginning with dead organic matter and driven by decomposers (saprotrophs).
The mass of living organisms (biomass) or number present in a unit area at a given time.
Only about 10% of the energy of one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost, mostly as heat.
A graphical representation of the food/energy relationship between trophic levels in terms of number, biomass or energy.
Consumer biomass exceeds producer biomass, e.g., in the sea where phytoplankton standing crop is small but fish biomass is large.
Storage and movement of nutrient elements through ecosystem components; gaseous (carbon, reservoir atmosphere) or sedimentary (phosphorus, reservoir Earth's crust).
